The long-term prognosis for patients with thymoma generally depends on several factors including tumor stage at diagnosis; however, it tends to be more favorable than that of thymic carcinoid when detected early (stage I). Thymomas have an overall 5-year survival rate ranging from approximately 70% to over 90%, depending on these stages. For invasive thymic carcinomas, which include both type A and B subtypes as per World Health Organization classification, the prognosis can vary widely but typically has lower survival rates compared to thymoma due in part to their aggressiveness—with average 5-year survival rates around 24%. It's important to note individual patient circumstances such as age, general health status, response to treatment, etc., also play significant roles in determperining specific cases’ outcomes. Overall though, while there exist effective treatments available leading many individuals towards remission, some may face recurrence necessitating further intervention. Thus, although not uniformly 'favorable', advancements continue improving management strategies enhancing life expectancy post-diagnosis.

The most frequent initial sign or symptom of urethral cancer can be blood in urine (hematuria), which may appear as pink-tinged to dark red urine. Other possible indications include difficulty during urination such as weak stream, intermittency, straining while voiding, dysuria (painful urination) due to inflammation caused by tumor growth within the narrow confines of the urethra; recurrent urinary tract infections that do not resolve with standard treatment might also suggest an underlying malignancy like urethral carcinoma. It's important for individuals experienning these symptoms to seek prompt evaluation from healthcare professionals who will likely perform diagnostic tests including cystoscopy wherein they insert a thin tube equipped with a camera into the bladder through the urethra to visualize any abnormalities directly. Biopsy procedures would then confirm diagnosis if suspicious lesions were identified. Early detection plays a crucial role in successful management outcomes hence awareness about potential warning signals should nevertheless encourage timely consultative assessments even when asymptomatic but at higher risk groups e.g., those having history of chronic irritation/inflammatory conditions affecting genitourinary system among others.

ClinicalTrials.gov is an excellent resource to search for active, recruiting, completed, and terminated clinical trials related to any condition including urethral cancer. To access this database, visit www.clinicaltrials.gov, enter "urethral cancer" in the search bar, and review the list of relevant studies along with their statuses (active/recruitment openings), locations, eligibility criteria, etc. Additionally, you may consult databases like PubMed Central or Embase which contain published articles summarizing trial results as well as other scientific literature regarding urologic malignancies such as urethral cancer. Always ensure that your sources come from reputed institutions or peer-reviewed journals when seeking out detailed study data or conclusions drawn by these investigations.

Vulvar cancer staging follows the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system which includes Stage I to IV. 

- **Stage I** involves tumors confined to the external genitalia or perineum that have not spread beyond immediate tissues; subdivided into IA without palpable inguinal nodes and IB with clinically involved lymph nodes.

- **Stage II** indicates extension from primary site onto adjacent structures like lower urethra but no involvement above this level nor distant metastasis.

- In **Stage III**, there's local invasion greater than stage II including pelvic sidewall/lymph node involvement, fixed fallopian tubes with positive nodes, or both labium majora affected by disease extending more proximally towards midline while still lacking distant metastases.

- Finally, **Stage IV** represents either regional lymphatic spread involving iliac lymph nodes or further afield such as paraaortic nodal enlargement plus possible visceral organ infilperation along with potential for distantly disseminated lesions throughout body systems.

People with an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm may not experience any specific symptoms until it becomes large enough to cause pain in their back or side of the stomach area if ruptured. However, some individuals might report deep, constant aching; sudden severe spots of pain that can radiate to other parts like legs (if thrombus is present); pulsating feeling near navel when lying down; clammy skin; dizziness/fainting due to internal bleeding from potential rupture. It's important for at-risk populations to have regular screenings as many AAA cases remain undetected without imaging studies since they often don’t produce early warning signs.

Abetalipoproteinemia is caused by mutations in the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) gene leading to impaired lipid absorption and transportation of dietary fats from the intestines. It's an autosomal recessive disorder; thus, individuals must inherit two defective copies of this gene—one from each parent—to manifest symptoms. There isn’t typically an "acquired" form as most cases result directly from genetic inheritance.

Typical symptoms of Alström Syndrome (previously known as Erickson's or ABRUZO disease) include progressive vision loss due to cone rod dystrophy, obesity leading to type 2 diabetes mellitus, insulin resistance, hyperlipidemptaemia with increased risk for cardiovascular diseases, sensorineural hearing impairment, dilated cardiomyopathy resulting in heart failure, polyuria/polydipsia from nephronophthisis causing chronic kidney disease, short stature, premature pubarche, hepatomegaly secondary to nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, endocrinal abnormalities such as hypogonadism, testicular atrophy, ovarian cysts, polycystic ovary syndrome, acanthosis nigricans, alopecia, dental caries, gingivitis, periodontitis, skeletal anomalies like scoliosis, kyphoscoliosis, joint laxity, flat feet, etc., skin changes like keratosis pilaris, palmar erythema, spider angiomas; some patients also exhibit behavioral issues, learning disabilities, attention deficits, psychiatric disturbances, sleep apnea, nocturnal enuresis,

Acanthomas typically do not require treatment unless they cause discomfort or cosmetic concerns; in such cases, topical corticosteroids may be prescribed to reduce inflammation. In most instances, an acanthoma will resolve spontaneously without intervention over time. However, if there is uncertainty about diagnosis or persistent symptoms, consulting with a dermatologist is recommended.

An accessory navicular is an extra (accessory) bone that can be found within the tendons above the arch of the foot. Typical symptoms include localized pain at the site where this small bony growth connects to the main part of your tibia through fibrous tissue; discomfort may increase with activity such as running or jumping due to irritation from shoes rubbing against the area. Some individuals might also experience mild swelling around the affected region during periods when they're active or after prolonged standing/walking. However, not everyone experiences these issues—some people have no symptoms whatsoever despite having an accessory navicular. It varies greatly among those who do feel effects related to its presence.

Aceruloplasminemia is typically diagnosed through genetic testing that identifies mutations in the CP gene responsible for this condition. Additionally, laboratory findings may include low serum ceruloplasmin levels (<10 mg/dL), high iron concentration with normal transferrin saturation, increased hepatic copper content upon liver biopsy, MRI showing cerebellar atrophy, and evidence of diabetes if present. Bloodwork often includes complete blood count, fasting glucose level, HbA1c test, ferritin measurement, as well as imaging studies like an abdominal ultrasound assessing organomegaly due to hemosiderosis.

Treatment options for achalasia aim to relieve symptoms by reducing lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure or stretching it open so that food can pass into the stomach more easily. The main treatments include pneumatic dilation, which involves using an endoscope with inflated balloons to forcefully dilate the LES; botulinum toxin injections directly into the LES muscle causing temporary paralysis of the muscles thereof facilitating easier passage of foods; surgical myotomy where longitudinal cuts are made through the inner circular layer of the LES via laparoscopy or thoracoscopically allowing permanent reduction in resting tone at this junction; pharmacological therapy like calcium channel blockers may be used but is less effective compared to other interventions mentioned above as these medications only provide modest relaxation of the LES without addressing underlying structural issues. These methods help restore normal peristalsis upwards from the body of the esophagus towards the mouth while simultaneously decreasing resistance offered by the non-relaxed LES during deglutition thereby improving overall swallow function.

Achondrogenesis is typically an autosomal recessive disorder; therefore, parents who carry one copy of the mutated gene may not show symptoms but have a 25% chance with each pregnancy to pass both copies onto their child if they're carriers for this condition. However, most cases result from new (de novo) genetic changes in affected individuals without any family history due to spontaneous mutations during gamete formation or early embryonic development.

Achondrogenesis Type II is an extremely rare lethal form of dwarfism characterized by severe skeletal abnormalities that typically result in stillbirth or death shortly after birth due to respiratory failure from underdeveloped lungs (pulmonary hypoplasia). Symptoms include shortened limbs with markedly reduced bone growth particularly noticeable at the long bones such as femurs and humeri; disproportionate body size where head circumference may be normal but trunk length significantly shorter than expected for gestational age; flat face profile; small chest cavity contributing to pulmonary complications; club feet might also occur. It's caused by mutations in genes responsible for cartilage formation during fetal development like COL10A1 gene encoding collagen X which plays a crucial role in endochondral ossification process. Diagnosis can often be made prenatally through ultrasound findings consistent with these characteristics coupled with molecular testing if available postnatally confirmed via radiographic imaging showing characteristic phenotypic traits mentioned above along with specific laboratory tests identifying causative genetic variants when possible. There’s no cure currently known nor treatment options beyond supportive care aimed primarily towards managing associated breathing difficulties until natural demise occurs soon thereafter given severity nature this condition presents itself within affected

The standard treatment approach for individuals with achondroplasia includes growth hormone therapy during childhood to increase height potential; however, its effectiveness is limited in this condition due to genetic factors affecting bone development. Surgical interventions may be necessary to correct skeletal abnormalities such as spinal stenosis or bowed legs (osteotomies). Additionally, supportive care including physical therapy can help improve mobility and muscle strength while addressing any complications that arise from disproportionate limb lengths. Regular monitoring by healthcare professionals specializing in pediatric endocrinology and orthopedics is recommended throughout life.

Acquired Hemophilia A (AHA) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by spontaneous bleeding due to antibodies against factor VIII, which leads to its inhibition or destruction. Unlike congenital hemophilia that's inherited genetically, individuals with AHA have no family history of the disease but acquire this condition later in life through unknown mechanisms possibly involving immunological dysregulation triggered by factors such as pregnancy, cancer, medications like antihypertensives, or other underlying diseases. Diagnosis involves detecting reduced levels of functional clotting factor VIII alongside high titers of specific IgG type inhibitors during coagulation tests. Acrocapitofemoral dysplasia typically presents with asymmetric shortening or underdevelopment (dwarfism) affecting mainly the upper arms, thighs, hands, and feet; joint pain may also be present in affected areas due to abnormal bone growth.

Scoliosis is common in individuals with achondroplasia due to their unique bone growth patterns. Symptoms include uneven shoulders or waistline where one side appears higher than the other; prominent ribs when breathing if thoracic spine involvement occurs (rib hump); back pain that may worsen over time as curvature progresses; limited mobility or discomfort during movement. It typically presents itself most noticeably between ages 10-2 years old but can be detected earlier through physical examination by healthcare providers who will observe these asymmetries along with radiographic imaging confirmation. Regular monitoring helps manage progression effectively.

Acromegaly is an endocrine disorder that results from excess growth hormone (GH) after skeletal maturation, primarily caused by benign pituitary adenomas producing GH or less commonly due to non-pituitary tumors secreting ectopic GH/growth factors. When developing, this condition leads to abnormal enlargement of various tissues such as bones and soft tissue; common symptoms include coarsened facial features, increased hand and foot size, joint pain, thick skin, deepening voice, sleep apnea, headaches, vision problems if there's pressure on optic nerves, insulin resistance leading potentially to diabetes, cardiovascptaular disease risk increase, etc., significantly impacting quality of life and increasing morbidity risks without treatment.

Acromesomelic Dysplasia, Maroteaux Type (AMDMT) is characterized by short stature with disproportionally shorter limbs compared to trunk length; specifically affecting hands and feet bones' growth. Other features include joint deformities such as hip displacement or clubfoot, underdeveloped clavicles leading to limited shoulder movement, flat facial profile due to midface hypoplasia, dental abnormalities like delayed eruption patterns, thickened skin particularly over knuckles resembling 'claw hand,' spinal curvature issues including scoliosis or kyphosis, hearing loss that may be conductive in nature initially but progressively sensorineural, heart valve problems notably mitral regurgitation which could lead to congestive cardiomyopathy later in life, umbilical hernias present at birth, reduced muscle tone causing floppiness especially noticeable during infancy when lifted from ground ('rag doll') effect, increased risk for respiratory complications secondary to chest wall structure anomalies impacting lung development/function, potential gastrointestinal tract malformation resulting in feeding difficulties early after birth requiring special nutritional support strategies tailored individually per patient needs - often involving tube feeds directly into stomach via nasogastric tubes inserted through nostril upwards towards esoph

Acute alcohol sensitivity refers to an individual's heightened reaction or adverse response after consuming even small amounts of alcoholic beverages. This can manifest as symptoms like facial flushing, nausea, rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), headache, low blood pressure, vertigo, unsteadiness, respiratory reactions such as wheezing in asthmatics, skin redness/flushing due to vasodilation caused by ethanol-induced release of histamine from mast cells, hypotension resulting in syncope, sweating, tremor, thirst leading to water drinking which may cause dilutional hyponatraemia, confusion, agitation, anxiety, irritability, full body pain without clear focus, abdominal discomfort with no evidence of ulceration, diarrhea, emesis followed later by tiredness lasting for days during withdrawal period despite having consumed only very little alcohol compared to others who do not experience these effects at all. It is important that individuals experiencing this condition seek professional advice regarding their consumption habits.

The standard treatment approach for acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (also known as Sweet's syndrome) typically includes systemic corticosteroids like prednisone to reduce inflammation quickly. In some cases where steroid use is contraindicated or if there’s an underlying malignancy associated with the condition, other options such as potassium iodide, colchicine, dapsone, or immunosuppressive agents may be considered. It's important that patients consult their healthcare provider for personalized management plans.

Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) is typically suspected in patients presenting with neurological symptoms such as abdominal pain or psychiatric disturbances without obvious cause. Diagnosis involves measuring urinary pyrroles during an attack; elevated levels suggest AIP. Definitive testing includes quantitative analysis of enzyme activity for hydroxymethylbilane synthase in erythroid cells obtained through venipuncture followed by culture to induce differentiation into red blood cell precursors where this enzyme should be active if normal. Genetic sequencing can identify mutations associated with AIP but isn't always necessary since treatment doesn’t depend solely upon genotype identification. Distinguishing AIP from similar disorders relies heavily on clinical presentation alongside these specific biochemical assays rather than imaging studies which may not show characteristic findings unique to AIP.

ADCY5-related dyskinesia is an autosomal dominant movement disorder characterized by involuntary movements (dyskinesias) such as chorea or dystonia that typically begin in childhood to early adolescence. It's caused by mutations in the gene encoding for Adenylyl cyclase type 5 enzyme which plays a role in neurotransmitter signaling within the brain. The condition can impact daily activities due to uncontrolled muscle contractions but varies widely among individuals affected. Treatment options may include medication like antiepileptic drugs or botulinum toxin injections depending upon symptoms severity and response.
Adenocarcinoma of the appendix means malignant tumors originating from glandular tissue within the appendix; yes, it's a form of cancer starting specifically in the appendix.

Adenoid cytic carcinoma is not typically considered to be an inherited cancer; most cases occur sporadically without any clear familial pattern or genetic predisposition identified as of my last update. However, like many cancers, there may still be some risk factors that could contribute indirectly through family history such as shared environmental exposures or lifestyle habits rather than directly inheritable mutations specific for this type of tumor. It's always recommended individuals discuss their personal risks with healthcare providers who have access to updated information about potential new findings related to inheritance patterns.

Typical symptoms of Adiposis dolorosa (also known as Dercum's disease) include multiple non-cancerous fatty lumps or lipomas that develop underneath the skin in various parts of the body such as arms, legs, trunk, face, hands, feet, fingers, toes, neck, shoulders, chest wall, back, buttocks, abdomen, hips, thighs, groin area, genitals, breasts, nipples, scrotum, penis, vulva, vagina, anus, rectal region, perineum, pubic bone areas, umbilicus, navel regions, lower belly button, upper inner thighs near pelvic/hip joints, knee caps, calves, shins, heels, arches, insteps, forearms, elbows, wrists, palm sides & fingertips, thumb bases, knuckle pads, finger tips, ring finger side nail bed edges; severe chronic localized pain within these growths which may be constant or intermittent with varying intensity levels ranging from mild discomfort up to excruciating agony causing significant distress affecting daily activities like walking, sitting, standing, lying down etc.; tenderness upon touch due to sensitivity around affected sites leading to difficulty during physical exam

ADNP Syndrome (Activity-Dependent Neurobehavioral Disorder with Pituitary Hypoplasia) is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations of the TFMT gene or its regulatory elements that lead to reduced levels of activity-dependent transcript regulator protein NAP1/ADNP. Individuals affected often present early developmental delays, intellectual impairment, hypotonia at birth progressing into hypertonicity later, seizures, dysmorphic facial features such as midface retrusion, almond-shaped eyes, high arched palate, micrognathism, thin upper lip vermillion border, small chin, low nasolabial folds, prominent ears, short stature, pigmentation anomaly like white forelock hair etc., behavior issues including anxiety, aggression, self-harm tendencies along with sleep disturbances among others. Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation supported by genetic testing confirming pathogenic variants within this specific locus. Management strategies focus primarily around symptoms' alleviation through multidisciplinary approach involving physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech & language intervention, educational support, psychological counseling, pharmacotherapy if needed alongside regular monitoring growth parameters, hormonal status especially thyroid function tests given hypothyroid

Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis has some genetic components but is not directly inherited like Mendelian traits; however, having family members with scoliosis may increase an individual's risk of developing the condition.

Typical symptoms of Down syndrome include distinct facial features (flattened face, upward slanting eyes), hypotonia at birth leading to delayed motor development, cognitive impairment ranging from mild to moderate intellectual disability, congenital heart defects, gastrointestinal anomalies like duodenal atresia or Hirschsprung disease, increased risk for leukemia, thyroid dysfunctions, hearing problems due to middle ear effusions, obstructive sleep apnea, immune deficiencies making them prone to respiratory tract infections, early-onset Alzheimer's disease, shorter stature with broad hands and feet having single palmar creases. In adults, while these core characteristics remain consistent, some may improve over time such as muscle tone; however, others might become more pronounced later in life including susceptibility to depression, social challenges, infertility issues predominantly affecting males, osteoporosis, hypothyroidism requiring lifelong monitoring, cardiac conditions necessitating regular checkups, and an elevated incidence of certain cancers particularly breast cancer by age 50. Early intervention programs focusing on speech therapy, physical therapy, occupational therapy, special education tailored towards individual needs help maximize their potential throughout adulthardom. Adult-onset vitelliform macular dystrophy commonly presents with central visual distortion (metamorphopsia), difficulty reading fine print due to loss in sharpness of sight, sensitivity to bright light, reduced color perception especially distinguishing between yellows and greens, and may eventually lead to scotomas which can cause blind spots within one's field of view. It does not usually result in complete blindness but progressive worsening over time is typical; early stages might be asymptomatic aside from subtle changes detected during an eye examination by retinal imaging techniques like OCT. Blurriness isn’t always present initially but could develop as lesions grow larger affecting more cone cells responsible for detailed central vision. Unusual yellowish egg-yolk shaped deposits called "vitreous" formations underneath the retina at the fovea where they disrupt normal photoreceptor function leading to these characteristic signs.

Afibrinogenemia typically presents with spontaneous bleeding episodes that can range from mild to severe hemorrhages such as nosebleeds (epistaxis), gum bleeding, easy bruising, prolonged menstruation in women, or excessive postoperative bleeding. In infants, umbilical cord separation may be delayed due to this condition. Severe cases might experience life-threatening internal bleeding after trauma or surgery. It is an inherited disorder characterized by extremely low levels or absence of fibrinogen leading to impaired blood clot formation. Diagnosis often involves coagulation tests showing significantly reduced plasma fibrinogen level along with genetic testing for mutations affecting FGA gene responsible for producing fibrinogen alpha chain. Treatment generally includes replacement therapy using cryoprecipitate or recombinant products containing high concentrates of fibrinogen during bleeding events or before surgerpta procedures. Prophylactic treatment regimens have also been used successfully in some patients. Regular monitoring and management under hematology specialists' guidance remain crucial aspects of care for individuals affected by afibrinogenemia.

Total Intestinal Aganglionic Megacolon (TIA), also known as Hirschsprung's disease in its most severe form affecting all colonic segments, presents with chronic constipation that begins shortly after birth or within few weeks to months postpartum; abdominal distension/bloating due to bowel obstruction; failure to pass meconium for more than 48 hours in newborns; vomiting which may be bilious if there is an associated small bowel involvement; enterocolitis characterized by fever, diarrhea, mucus, blood in stool, lethargy indicating possible inflammation of the affected segment(s); poor weight gain despite adequate caloric intake; rectal prolapse can occur but it’s less common compared to other forms of Hirschsprung Disease. Diagnosis often involves radiographic imaging such as contrast enema studies showing transition zone between normal and diseased tissue along with confirmatory biopsies demonstrating absence of ganglion cells from myenteric plexus. Treatment typically requires surgical resection of the non-functioning portion of the gut followed by reanastomosing healthy sections together.

Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome Type 1 (AGS) is an inherited genetic disorder that primarily affects the brain, immune system, and skin. It's classified as one of several types within the broader category known as "leukodystrophies," which involve abnormalities in myelin – the protective covering around nerve fibers. Diagnosing someone with this condition means they have mutations in specific genes like TREX1 or RNASEH2B/C causing early childhood symptoms such as encephalopathy, liver dysfunction, dermatitis, and distinctive white matter changes visible through neuroimaging techniques. The prognosis varies but often involves severe developmental delays and progressively worsening neurological issues over time. There’s currently no cure for AGS; treatment focuses mainly on managing individual symptoms to improve quality of life.

The typical symptoms and early signs of Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome Type 3 (AGS) include chronic cerebrospinal venous insufficiency with associated features such as encephalopathy characterized by irritability, lethargy or hypotonia in infancy; elevated levels of interferon alpha activity leading to hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, dermatitis resembling congenital cutaneous ichthyosis, alopecia, nail dystrophy, pneumonitis, thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia, cataracts, retinopathy, micrognathism, dental abnormalities, growth delay, intellectual disabilities, seizures, psychiatric disturbances like autistic behaviors, recurrent fever episodes without obvious cause, arteriosclerosis, calcifications within brain parenchyma visible through imaging studies, and white matter changes suggestive of demyelination/leukodystrophies seen via MRI scans. It typically presents during childhood but can be diagnosed earlier depending upon clinical manifestations' severity. Diagnosis is confirmed using genetic testing for mutations in TREX1 gene among others implicated in this condition. Early recognition facilitates management aimed towards

Ainhum (also known as dactylolysis spontanea) is a rare disease that affects primarily individuals of African descent; it involves progressive constriction or "ring" formation around one toe leading to its eventual autoamputation due to vascular compromise from fibrosing bands encircling peripheral digits. The name 'ainhum' originates from Yoruba language meaning “to shrink” which describes the characteristic feature of the disorder - gradual narrowing of affected digit(usually fifth toe). It typically presents with painless swelling followed by skin changes such as thickening, hyperkeratosis, ulceration, and ultimately amputation if left untreated. Its exact etiology remains unclear but may involve genetic predisposition combined with environmental factors like footwear pressure contributing towards localized trauma-induced pathological response within soft tissues surrounding involved phalanges. Diagnosis relies heavily upon clinical examination supported occasionally through imaging modalities including X-ray/MRI for assessment extent & severity while treatment options range broadly depending individual case specifications encompass conservative measures up till surgical intervention involving debridement procedures aimed at relieving symptomatic relief along prevention further complications associated therewith.

Alagille syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder characterized by liver dysfunction due to bile duct paucity (reduced number of intrahepatic bile ducts), which can lead to jaundice; it also involves heart defects such as peripheral pulmonic stenosis or tetralogy of Fallot, skeletal abnormalities like butterfly vertebrae, ocular anomalies including posterior embryotoxon in eyes, distinctive facial features with deep-set eyes and pointed chin, along with potential kidney problems and vascus arcus corneae. It's caused primarily by mutations in the JAG1 gene, less commonly in NOTCH2. Diagnosis often includes clinical evaluation supported by imaging studies for hepatobiliary system assessment and echocardiography for cardiac issues. Management focuses on treating symptoms and complications related to organ systems involved.

Yes, Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (AHO) is caused by mutations in the GNAS gene that encodes for the alpha subunit of stimulatory G protein involved in signal transduction pathways related to growth hormone release among others. It's an autosomal dominant disorder with variable expressivity due to its imprinting pattern; typically only maternal alleles affect phenotype expression when inherited from affected mothers. This results in symptoms like short stature, brachydactyly, obesity, developmental delay or learning difficulties, as well as resistance to parathyroid hormone leading to hypocalcemia despite elevated levels of circulating PTH—a hallmark feature known as pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A if present without other AHO features but can also occur alongside them indicating pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism. Genetic testing confirms diagnosis through identification of specific methylation changes at this locus rather than sequencing alone since not all causative variants may be detected via sequence analysis given their complexity involving genomic imprinting mechanisms beyond simple nucleotide substitutions/deletions etc., necessitating specialized assays tailored towards detecting such epigenetically influenced alterations instead. Typically, individuals with Moynahan Syndrome present alopecia or hair loss as one prominent feature; however, it's important to note that this condition is not widely recognized in current literature under such name—it may be confused with other genetic conditions affecting multiple systems like neurofibromatosis type 1 which can cause café-au-lait spots along with learning disabilities but does not typically involve seizures unless there’s an associated brain tumor known as optic glioma. Epileptic episodes could occur due to various reasons unrelated directly to these rare syndromes if they were indeed part of their presentation. Oligophrenia refers outdated terminology for intellectual disability, suggesting cognitive impairment might also characterize the hypothetical "Moynahan Syndrome." However, without specific details about diagnostic criteria or prevalence rates from authoritative sources, providing accurate information regarding 'typical symptoms,' 'clinical features', or even confirmation of existence remains challenging. It would be best advised to consult up-to-date resources or specialists when dealing with unusual combinations of symptoms potentially indicative of complex multifactorial diseases.

Alopecia Universalis (AU) is an advanced form of alopecia areata characterized by total scalp hair loss as well as extensive body hair loss; however, AU does not cause hair to grow back in other parts of the skin or lead to widespread bodily symptoms beyond localized areas where hair follicles become dormant due to immune system attacks against them. It's considered primarily autoimmune rather than infectious or hereditary diseases causing full-body hairlessness like congenital generalized hypertrichosis lanuginosa which leads to excessive growth instead of absence of all types of hair across the whole body surface except palms and soles.

Treatment options for Alopecia Universalis (AU) include corticosteroids, minoxidil topical application, immunotherapy with diphenylcyclopropenone, JAK inhibitors like tofacitinib citrate, as well as potential future gene-targeted therapies such as Janus kinase 1/2 pathway modulators. Effectiveness varies among individuals; some may experience hair regrowth while others do not respond significantly. It's important to consult healthcare professionals before starting treatment due to possible side effects.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is caused by genetic mutations inherited from one's parents; specifically, defective SERPINA1 gene variants lead to reduced levels of AAT protein which protects tissues from enzyme damage. It is an autosomal codominant condition that individuals are born with rather than developing later in life.

Alpha-thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder characterized by reduced or absent production of α-globin chains that form part of hemoglobin in red blood cells (RBCs). This deficiency leads to less functional RBCs which can result in microcytosis (smaller than normal RBCs) and hypochromia (less color due to lowered hemoglobin content), causing mild to severe forms of anemia depending upon the number of affected genes. The severity ranges from silent carriers with no symptoms to Hemoglobin H disease where patients have moderate chronic anemia, up to hydrops fetalis—a lethal condition for infants if both parents pass down defective alleles. Treatment varies according to severity but may include regular transfusions, iron chelation therapy, folic acid supplements, and potentially bone marrow transplantation.

Typical signs and symptoms include microcephaly (small head size), developmental delay or intellectual disabilities, skeletal abnormalities such as metacarpopharyangeal joint contractures, distinctive facial features like frontal bossing, hypertelorism (wide spacing between eyes), epicanthic folds, and low nasolabial angle; some patients may also have heart defects or other organ anomalies. It is important to note that severity can vary widely among affected individuals.

Yes, Alport syndrome is typically an inherited condition that runs in families due to mutations in genes related to type IV collagen production; however, there have been rare cases of de novo (sporadic) occurrences where no family history exists. It most commonly follows X-linked recessive inheritance but also autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive patterns exist.

No, there seems to be no recognized medical condition called "Ambras Syndrome." It's possible that this term might have been confused with another disease or could potentially refer to an extremely rare disorder not widely documented in mainstream medicine as of my last update. Always consult healthcare professionals for accurate diagnoses and information about specific conditions.

Amelogenesis imperfecta is primarily an inherited disorder that affects tooth enamel development; however, there have been rare cases where mutations arise de novo (spontaneously) without being present in either parent's genetic material. It usually follows autosomal dominant inheritance but may also be recessive or X-linked depending on the type of gene affected.

The typical presentation for X-linked hypoplastic/hypo maturation amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) Type II includes enamel defects characterized by thin or absent tooth enamel that is prone to rapid wear and breakage; teeth may appear yellowish due to dentin exposure but can also have an opalescent sheen in some cases. Clinically, affected individuals often exhibit generalized moderate size with normal shaped crowns except for anterior central incisors which might be pegged laterally narrow and pointed at the mesial end. This condition usually presents during early childhood as primary teeth erupt abnormally. It's important to note this form of AI has been associated primarily with mutations affecting genes located on the X chromosome such as DLX3 gene. Diagnosis involves both clinical examination and radiographic analysis showing reduced thickness of enamel layer without alteration in pulp chamber shape. Genetic testing confirms diagnosis when indicated. Treatment focuses mainly on protective restorative care rather than cosmetic correction given its progressive nature.

Amniotic Band Syndrome (ABS) occurs when strands of the fetal membrane separate from one another during pregnancy but fail to dissolve or disperse within the womb as they normally would. These bands can entangle parts of the developing fetus causing constrictions that may lead to limb deformities, digits absence, craniofacial anomalies, organ malformation, or even miscarriage depending upon where these bands attach themselves. The exact cause remains unknown; however, ABS isn't believed to be hereditary nor caused by anything mothers did before knowing about their condition. It happens spontaneously at random with no clear risk factors identified yet. Treatment options vary according to severity ranging from physical therapy for minor cases to surgical interventives like FETO procedure which involves inserting tiny balloons into utero through ultrasound guidance under local anesthesia aiming to prevent further damage until birth allowing time for natural growth while minimizing risks associated with premature delivery.

AA amyloidosis (primary) is an autoimmune-related systemic disorder characterized by abnormal deposits of protein called "amyloid" in organs and tissues throughout the body leading to organ dysfunction or failure; It often results from chronically high levels of serum Amyloid A proteins due to inflammatrightarrows such as rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, familial Mediterranean fever etc.; The exact mechanism involves misfolding of these acute phase reactants into insoluble fibrils that accumulate within extracellular spaces causing damage over time.

Amyopathic dermatomyositis (ADM) is characterized by typical skin manifestations of dermatomyositis without clinical or laboratory evidence of muscle inflammation that would suggest myositis. In contrast to classic dermatomyositis which involves both cutaneous symptoms and progressive proximal muscle weakness due to underlying autoimmune-mediated muscle damage, ADM patients exhibit only the former with normal creatine kinase levels and no significant elevation in aldolase enzymes typically associated with active muscle disease. Diagnosis relies heavily upon imaging techniques such as MRI for detecting subclinical involvement since standard tests may not reveal overt signs of muscle pathology. The exact cause remains unclear but shares an immunological basis similar to other forms of idiopathptaic inflammatory myopathies. Treatment strategies often focus more intensively on managing skin lesions rather than addressing nonexistent muscular issues.

The exact cause of ALS is unknown; however, factors such as genetic mutations, environmental exposures, or abnormalities within cells that lead to motor neuron damage may contribute to its development. It's believed to be multifactorial with both hereditary and sporadic cases observed. Some individuals have familial forms due to specific gene mutations like SOD1, TDP-43, FUS, etc., while others might acquire nonfamilial types without clear inheritance patterns. Research continues into understanding all contributing elements for targeted therapages.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis-Parkinsonism/Dementia Complex Type 1 (ALS-PD) is characterized by progressive muscle weakness due to motor neuron degeneration leading to ALS; parkinsonian features such as bradykinesia, rigidity, tremors at rest; cognitive decline resulting in dementia with executive dysfunction being prominent early signs. It often starts subtly with asymmetric limb stiffness or clumsiness before advancing rapidly over months to years into more severe disability.

An anaplastic ganglioglioma is indeed a rare grade III malignant (anaplastic) variant of ganglioglioma that occurs primarily within the central nervous system; most commonly found in children or young adults but can also occur at any age. It's characterized by neoplasms with both glial cell and neuronal elements which tend to be more aggressive than typical low-grade gangliogliomas due to their higher mitotic activity and potential for recurrence after treatment. Yes, this condition represents a specific subtype of pediatric brain tumors often associated with seizures as they typically arise from cortical regions involved in epileptogenesis.

Common symptoms of Andersen-Tawil Syndrome include periodic paralysis (intermittent episodes where muscles become weak or unable to contract), cardiac arrhythmias which may lead to palpitations or fainting spells, distinctive facial features such as prominent everted eyes with upward slanting outer lids, low set ears, pointed chin, thin upper lip, small mouth, dental abnormalities like high arches in teeth, skeletal anomalies including clinodactyly (curved fingers) particularly pinkie finger towards thumb side, camptodactyly (permanently bent digits), scoliosis, short stature, delayed development/speech delay, genital hypoplasia in males leading to infertility issues due to undescended testicles at birth that fail to descend properly into the scrotum by puberty timeframe; females experience oligomenorrhea resulting from polycystic ovary disease causing irregular menstruation cycles along with hirsutism - excess hair growth over body parts typically seen only during female sexual maturation phase post adolescence period characterized primarily through breast enlargement & distribution pattern changes within axillary region i.e., underarm area).

Spinocerebellar Ataxia Signs can be subtle initially then progressively worsen over time; early indicators involve clumsiness, unsteady gait leading to frequent falls, difficulty coordinating movements such as eating or writing ("dysdiadochokinesia"), slurred speech ("ataxic dysarthria") and abnormal eye movement patterns known as nystagmus. Genetic testing is definitive since it's usually inherited disorders caused by mutation(s) affecting proteins involved in cellular functions within nervous system cells predominantly located in the cerebellum which controls balance & coordination.

Anencephaly is characterized by missing brain tissue in newborns; infants with this condition typically have no cerebral cortex or skull vault above their brainstem. Symptoms include absence of parts of the brain (cerebrum), scalp defects at birth due to incomplete closure of neural tubes during development. Infants usually do not survive more than a few hours after birth as they lack essential structures for life functions such as breathing and feeding autonomously.

Most cases of Angelman syndrome result from random genetic mutations in the maternal copy of chromosome 15 during early development; they do not typically inherit this condition directly from their parents but rather experience de novo (new) occurrences. However, about one-third may be due to inheriting an abnormality called UBE3A gene imprinting defects from a mother who carries them without showing symptoms herself because she has two copies of the normal gene—one active and one silenced by imprinting. This is known as inheritance through uniparental disomy when both copies come from the father instead of having one each from both parents.

The treatment of aniridia typically involves managing symptoms since there is no cure. Options include protective eyewear to shield from UV light due to increased sensitivity; prescription glasses or contact lenses if refractive errors occur; surgical interventions like cataract extraction when necessary; glaucoma medications as individuals with aniridia have higher risk; regular monitoring by ophthalmologists specializing in retinal diseases given associated risks such as keratopathy and nystagmus. Genetic counseling may also be recommended considering its hereditary nature.

Ankylosing spondylitis has been observed with familial clustering suggesting genetic predisposition; however, not all cases can be explained by inheritance alone as environmental factors also play a role. The HLA-B27 gene is associated with increased risk but its presence doesn't guarantee disease development or transmission of symptoms within family members due to incomplete penetrance.

Anonychia congenital is a rare genetic disorder characterized by complete absence of nails from birth (congenitally). It can occur as part of various syndromes or independently. Individuals with this condition lack both fingernails and toenails entirely; however, they typically do not experience any additional symptoms related to their health beyond the missing nail structures themselves unless associated with other systemic conditions. The exact cause involves mutations affecting keratin proteins essential for normal nail development during embryogenesis. Treatment focuses primarily on protective measures since there's no cure that restores natural nail growth.

Anophthalmia-Plus Syndromes encompass various genetic disorders characterized by underdeveloped or absent eyes (anophthalmos) along with additional anomalies in other parts of the body. Typical symptoms include missing irises, small eye sockets without visible eyeballs, colobomas which may appear as notches at the edge of structures like ears or lips, cleft palate, hearing loss, intellectual disability, limb abnormalities such as shortened fingers, heart defects, kidney problems, growth delays, distinct facial appearance including widely spaced eyes if present, broad nasal bridge, low set ears, etc. The severity varies among individuals; some might have mild effects while others could experience significant developmental challenges impacting their quality of life. Diagnosis is often made through clinical examination supported by imaging techniques and confirmed via genetic testing for associated mutations. Management involves multidisciplinary care addressing each individual's specific needs to optimize health outcomes and supportive therapages aimed at improving functional capabilities.

Anterior polar cataracts typically present as small white opacities located at the front (central) part of the lens inside the eye. They may not significantly affect vision initially but can lead to blurred vision over time. Symptoms include decreased visual acuity, glare sensitivity, especially when facing bright lights like headlights at night, difficulty with reading fine print, and sometimes monocular diplopia where one sees double images through only one affected eye. The severity depends on size and density; some individuals might be asymptomatic for years before any change is noticed. Regular ophthalmologic evaluations help monitor progression.

Antisynthetase syndrome is caused by autoantibodies targeting aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases enzymes; its development may be linked to genetic predisposition combined with environmental factors that trigger an abnormal immune response in susceptible individuals.

Aplasia cutis congenita is a rare condition where an individual has missing skin at birth; typically affecting areas such as the scalp but can occur elsewhere on the body. It ranges in severity from small patches to large sections of absent skin. The exact cause remains unknown, though it may be associated with genetic factors or disruptions during fetal development. Treatment depends on the size and location of the affected area and might include wound care management for minor cases while more severe instances could require surgical intervention.

Autosomal recessive aplasia cutis congenita (ACC) typically presents at birth with localized absence or deficiency of skin primarily affecting the scalp but may also involve other parts such as extremities like hands and feet. The affected areas appear smooth and hairless compared to surrounding normal tissue without underlying bone involvement in most cases. Complications include potential for secondary wound complications due to trauma exposure since there is no protective layer; however, severe systemic issues related directly to ACC itself do not usually occur unless associated abnormalities exist outside this condition's scope.

Aquagenic pruritus is caused by an abnormal reaction of the skin to sweat or moisture from exposure to water; however, its exact pathophysiology remains unclear. Some theories suggest that mast cells release histamine in response to water stimuli leading to intense itching without visible hives for those affected. It's not fully understood why only certain individuals experience this condition but may involve genetic predisposition combined with environmental factors.
reference_answers: Key Points - Adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - Previous chemotherapy and exposure to radiation may increase the risk of developing ALL. - Signs and symptoms of adult ALL include fever, feeling tired, and easy bruising or bleeding. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult ALL. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). Adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL; also called acute lymphocytic leukemia) is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. This type of cancer usually gets worse quickly if it is not treated. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. - Granulocytes (white blood cells) that fight infection and disease. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a lymphoblast cell and then one of three types of lymphocytes (white blood cells): - B lymphocytes that make antibodies to help fight infection. - T lymphocytes that help B lymphocytes make the antibodies that help fight infection. - Natural killer cells that attack cancer cells and viruses. In ALL, too many stem cells become lymphoblasts, B lymphocytes, or T lymphocytes. These cells are also called leukemia cells. These leukemia cells are not able to fight infection very well. Also, as the number of leukemia cells increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may cause infection, anemia, and easy bleeding. The cancer can also spread to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). This summary is about adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia. See the following PDQ summaries for information about other types of leukemia: - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment. - Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treatment. - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment. - Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Treatment. - Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia Treatment. - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment.

Key Points - Once adult ALL has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) or to other parts of the body. - There is no standard staging system for adult ALL. Once adult ALL has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) or to other parts of the body. The extent or spread of cancer is usually described as stages. It is important to know whether the leukemia has spread outside the blood and bone marrow in order to plan treatment. The following tests and procedures may be used to determine if the leukemia has spread: - Chest x-ray : An x-ray of the organs and bones inside the chest. An x-ray is a type of energy beam that can go through the body and onto film, making a picture of areas inside the body. - Lumbar puncture : A procedure used to collect a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spinal column. This is done by placing a needle between two bones in the spine and into the CSF around the spinal cord and removing a sample of the fluid. The sample of CSF is checked under a microscope for signs that leukemia cells have spread to the brain and spinal cord. This procedure is also called an LP or spinal tap. - CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of the abdomen, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly. This procedure is also called computed tomography, computerized tomography, or computerized axial tomography. - MRI (magnetic resonance imaging): A procedure that uses a magnet, radio waves, and a computer to make a series of detailed pictures of areas inside the body. This procedure is also called nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI). There is no standard staging system for adult ALL. The disease is described as untreated, in remission, or recurrent. Untreated adult ALL The ALL is newly diagnosed and has not been treated except to relieve signs and symptoms such as fever, bleeding, or pain. - The complete blood count is abnormal. - More than 5% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are signs and symptoms of leukemia. Adult ALL in remission The ALL has been treated. - The complete blood count is normal. - 5% or fewer of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are no signs or symptoms of leukemia other than in the bone marrow.

Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult AML. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as lumps or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC): A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the sample made up of red blood cells. - Peripheral blood smear : A procedure in which a sample of blood is checked for blast cells, the number and kinds of white blood cells, the number of platelets, and changes in the shape of blood cells. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for signs of cancer. - Cytogenetic analysis : A laboratory test in which the cells in a sample of blood or bone marrow are viewed under a microscope to look for certain changes in the chromosomes. Other tests, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), may also be done to look for certain changes in the chromosomes. - Immunophenotyping : A process used to identify cells, based on the types of antigens or markers on the surface of the cell. This process is used to diagnose the subtype of AML by comparing the cancer cells to normal cells of the immune system. For example, a cytochemistry study may test the cells in a sample of tissue using chemicals (dyes) to look for certain changes in the sample. A chemical may cause a color change in one type of leukemia cell but not in another type of leukemia cell. - Reverse transcriptionpolymerase chain reaction test (RTPCR): A laboratory test in which cells in a sample of tissue are studied using chemicals to look for certain changes in the structure or function of genes. This test is used to diagnose certain types of AML including acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).

Key Points - Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - Older age can affect the risk of developing chronic lymphocytic leukemia. - Signs and symptoms of chronic lymphocytic leukemia include swollen lymph nodes and tiredness. - Tests that examine the blood, bone marrow, and lymph nodes are used to detect (find) and diagnose chronic lymphocytic leukemia. - Certain factors affect treatment options and prognosis (chance of recovery). Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (also called CLL) is a blood and bone marrow disease that usually gets worse slowly. CLL is one of the most common types of leukemia in adults. It often occurs during or after middle age; it rarely occurs in children. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the body makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - White blood cells that fight infection and disease. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a lymphoblast cell and then one of three types of lymphocytes (white blood cells): - B lymphocytes that make antibodies to help fight infection. - T lymphocytes that help B lymphocytes make antibodies to fight infection. - Natural killer cells that attack cancer cells and viruses. In CLL, too many blood stem cells become abnormal lymphocytes and do not become healthy white blood cells. The abnormal lymphocytes may also be called leukemia cells. The lymphocytes are not able to fight infection very well. Also, as the number of lymphocytes increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may cause infection, anemia, and easy bleeding. This summary is about chronic lymphocytic leukemia. See the following PDQ summaries for more information about leukemia: - Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment. - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment. - Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treatment. - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment. - Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia Treatment. - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment.

New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. This summary section describes treatments that are being studied in clinical trials. It may not mention every new treatment being studied. Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website. Chemotherapy with stem cell transplant Chemotherapy with stem cell transplant is a method of giving chemotherapy and replacing blood -forming cells destroyed by the cancer treatment. Stem cells (immature blood cells) are removed from the blood or bone marrow of the patient or a donor and are frozen and stored. After the chemotherapy is completed, the stored stem cells are thawed and given back to the patient through an infusion. These reinfused stem cells grow into (and restore) the bodys blood cells. Biologic therapy Biologic therapy is a treatment that uses the patient's immune system to fight cancer. Substances made by the body or made in a laboratory are used to boost, direct, or restore the body's natural defenses against cancer. This type of cancer treatment is also called biotherapy or immunotherapy. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy CAR T-cell therapy is a type of immunotherapy that changes the patient's T cells (a type of immune system cell) so they will attack certain proteins on the surface of cancer cells. T cells are taken from the patient and special receptors are added to their surface in the laboratory. The changed cells are called chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. The CAR T cells are grown in the laboratory and given to the patient by infusion. The CAR T cells multiply in the patient's blood and attack cancer cells. CAR T-cell therapy is being studied in the treatment of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Clinical trials are part of the cancer research process. Clinical trials are done to find out if new cancer treatments are safe and effective or better than the standard treatment. Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment. Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward. Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. There are also clinical trials that test new ways to stop cancer from recurring (coming back) or reduce the side effects of cancer treatment. Clinical trials are taking place in many parts of the country. See the Treatment Options section that follows for links to current treatment clinical trials. These have been retrieved from NCI's listing of clinical trials.

Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia.. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease such as an enlarged spleen. A history of the patients health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC) with differential : A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells and platelets. - The number and type of white blood cells. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the blood sample made up of red blood cells. - Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for abnormal cells. One of the following tests may be done on the samples of blood or bone marrow tissue that are removed: - Cytogenetic analysis: A test in which cells in a sample of blood or bone marrow are viewed under a microscope to look for certain changes in the chromosomes, such as the Philadelphia chromosome. - FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization): A laboratory technique used to look at genes or chromosomes in cells and tissues. Pieces of DNA that contain a fluorescent dye are made in the laboratory and added to cells or tissues on a glass slide. When these pieces of DNA bind to specific genes or areas of chromosomes on the slide, they light up when viewed under a microscope with a special light. - Reverse transcriptionpolymerase chain reaction (RTPCR): A laboratory test in which cells in a sample of tissue are studied using chemicals to look for certain changes in the structure or function of genes.

Key Points - Hairy cell leukemia is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - Gender and age may affect the risk of hairy cell leukemia. - Signs and symptoms of hairy cell leukemia include infections, tiredness, and pain below the ribs. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose hairy cell leukemia. - Certain factors affect treatment options and prognosis (chance of recovery). Hairy cell leukemia is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell). Hairy cell leukemia is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. This rare type of leukemia gets worse slowly or does not get worse at all. The disease is called hairy cell leukemia because the leukemia cells look "hairy" when viewed under a microscope. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - White blood cells that fight infection and disease. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a lymphoblast cell and then into one of three types of lymphocytes (white blood cells): - B lymphocytes that make antibodies to help fight infection. - T lymphocytes that help B lymphocytes make antibodies to help fight infection. - Natural killer cells that attack cancer cells and viruses. In hairy cell leukemia, too many blood stem cells become lymphocytes. These lymphocytes are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. They are also called leukemia cells. The leukemia cells can build up in the blood and bone marrow so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may cause infection, anemia, and easy bleeding. Some of the leukemia cells may collect in the spleen and cause it to swell. This summary is about hairy cell leukemia.
